own_scenes.family: Soul y proto-funk: Stax, Nueva Orleans, Motown
own_scenes.desc: El imperio de Otis Redding, Booker T & the MGs, Johnnie Taylor, Rufus y Carla Thomas, los Staple Singers, Isaac Hayes y Albert King, capaz de rivalizar con Motown en ventas, con un sonido campestre y frito más pensado para el público negro. Frente al montaje mecánico de Motown, en Stax se grababa todo junto: «toca lo que sientas» (Otis Redding). «Tramp» de Otis y Carla, con el bajo más grave de la radio, es proto-funk puro; Johnnie Taylor llevó la sordidez sexual al soul («Who’s Making Love», «Disco Lady» con Bootsy al bajo); Rufus Thomas, payaso de «Do the Funky Chicken», hizo un poco más aceptable ser funky. Los MGs eran groove fluido más que bomba funk («Hip Hug-Her», «Melting Pot»), y los Bar-Kays originales («Soul Finger») habrían sido reyes de Memphis si no hubieran muerto con Otis en 1967.

notes.chapter: Cap. 12: Power to the People: It’s Just Begun
notes.text: Tras la muerte de Otis y de King, Jim Stewart vendió Stax a su socio negro Al Bell, que la puso un momento en la cima: el concierto Wattstax en el Coliseo de Los Ángeles (agosto de 1972, a un dólar la entrada), con Isaac Hayes, Rufus Thomas, Albert King, los Staple Singers y los Bar-Kays («el nuevo funk de rock negro») y la invocación de Jesse Jackson que Public Enemy samplearía; y el disco That Nigger’s Crazy de Richard Pryor, un millón de copias sin radio. Pero la expansión y el fracaso del acuerdo con Columbia la llevaron a la quiebra en 1975: se acabó la era de los sellos independientes de R&B.

refs.q: The Memphis-based Stax Records was a cornerstone of the rhythm and blues to funk evolution.
refs.para: The Memphis-based Stax Records was a cornerstone of the rhythm and blues to funk evolution. The home of Otis Redding, Booker T & the MGs, Johnnie Taylor, the Mar-Keys, the Bar-Kays, Rufus Thomas, Carla Thomas, the Staple Singers, Isaac Hayes, Albert King, and others, Stax Records was a musical empire of the 1960s that could rival Motown in total record sales. Its down-home country-fried sound made it distinct, and probably not as completely appealing to the middle-class set, both black and white. Founded by the siblings Jim Stewart and Estelle Axton in 1960, the company exuded the easygoing demeanor of its bosses. Unlike their northern rhythm and blues counterparts, Stax producers welcomed performers, producers, custodians, secretaries, and executives to play important roles in developing a finished product. This cooperation and spontaneity contributed to the flavor of the Stax sound. Otis Redding explained the differences between Stax and the music-making corporation at Motown in an interview printed in Rolling Stone in 1968:
refs.chapter: Cap. 6: La revolución rítmica: Tighten Up

refs.q: Motown does a lot of overdubbing. It’s mechanically done.
refs.para: Motown does a lot of overdubbing. It’s mechanically done. At Stax the rule is: Whatever you feel, play it. We cut everything together, horns, rhythms, and vocal. We’ll do it over three or four times and listen to the results and pick the best one. If somebody doesn’t like a line in the song we’ll go back and cut the whole song over. Until last year, we didn’t even have a four-track tape recorder. You can’t overdub on a one-track machine.
refs.chapter: Cap. 6: La revolución rítmica: Tighten Up

refs.q: In perhaps the most representative tale of the rise and fall of independently produced funk, the legendary Stax Records flashed and burned
refs.para: In perhaps the most representative tale of the rise and fall of independently produced funk, the legendary Stax Records flashed and burned as a black-owned label in a few short years in the early 1970s. After enduring a chaotic reorganization in Memphis following the death of Otis Redding in late 1967, the assassination of Martin Luther King, Jr., in Memphis in April 1968, and subsequent racial disharmony at the label, cofounder Jim Stewart was ready to quit. Selling a portion of the label in 1968, Stewart bailed out and sold the label to his (black) partner, executive Al Bell. Bell had a lot of idealistic plans, although eventually the label went under. But for a hot minute, he had Stax on top of the black music scene.
refs.chapter: Cap. 12: Power to the People: It’s Just Begun

podcast.title: Signing of Delaney & Bonnie (1968)
podcast.body: In 1968, Delaney & Bonnie signed with the legendary Stax Records in Memphis, which influenced their music with a distinct soul sound. "In 1968 Delinean Bonnie signed with the legendary stacks records and Memphis and you can hear that soul influence in their music."

podcast.title: Early Post-Moman Struggles
podcast.body: After Chips Moman left, Stax "flounded a little bit for a few months." Jim Stewart and Steve Cropper shared production duties, releasing a mix of good but unsuccessful soul records and "truly die a novelty country songs" that failed to hit the charts. "After Momen left, the label flounded a little bit for a few months."

podcast.title: Market Research Advantage
podcast.body: The Stax studio, located in a former cinema, had a record shop in its lobby run by Estelle Axton. This allowed the label to conduct real-time market research by observing what black teenagers were buying and listening to, and even testing new recordings on the crowd. "By having a record shop in the record studio itself, they knew what was selling and could make more music that sounded like that."

podcast.title: Not Exclusively a Soul Label Initially
podcast.body: In its early days, Stax Records was not exclusively a soul label. It continued to cut country and rockabilly records, such as the session booked for Billy Lee Riley that accidentally led to the formation of Booker T and the M.G.'s. "Stacks were still not exclusively a soul label, and it was cutting the art country unrocketably record"

podcast.title: Origin from Satellite Records
podcast.body: Stax Records was born from Satellite Records after a trademark conflict. The name is an acronym formed from the first two letters of founders Jim Stewart and Estelle Axton's surnames. "Stax Records was born."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rapid Catalog Expansion
podcast.body: To quickly establish a new catalog after its split from Atlantic Records, Stax Records released an unprecedented 27 albums all at once. This strategy provided numerous artists, including Isaac Hayes, with the opportunity to create and release music, with Hayes notably insisting on doing it "his way." "Stacks records had split from Atlantic records and needed a catalog so they released 27 albums all at once to give them this quick catalog of music."

podcast.title: Split from Atlantic Records
podcast.body: Stax Records underwent a significant transition when it split from Atlantic Records. This separation necessitated a rapid strategy to rebuild its music catalog independently. "Stacks records had split from Atlantic records and needed a catalog."

podcast.title: The "Mixed Group" House Band
podcast.body: The success of "Green Onions" led to Booker T and the M.G.'s becoming the Stax house band, a significant development for the label. This group, with its "mixed" black and white members, played on virtually every session, providing a consistent and distinctive sound. "That Curg group became the stacks house band, playing on every session from that point on."
